newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Golden sunsets heralds red dawn in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Golden sunsets heralds red dawn in Hong Kong.

text.p: With only 100 days to go until the British colony of Hong Kong reverts to Communist-ruled China, even the most determined pessimist would be hard pressed to find physical evidence of a city on the rocks.
Despite the monumental political changes that are fast approaching, it is business as usual in Hong Kong, a wealthy, hardworking, hard-playing community of 6.4 million people.

In a tribute to its resilience, the death of China's leader Deng Xiaoping in February passed with barely a ripple. Fears that the stock market would collapse and that a terrified Hong Kong would withdraw into a protective shell while a power struggle raged in China proved unfounded.
There are no boarded up windows. There is no evidence of a frightened population preparing to steal way into the night, or of the panic, decay or neglect some doom-mongers had predicted.
To the contrary. It is virtually impossible to escape the cacophony of jackhammers, of round-the-clock construction and renovation that barely pauses for breath, even on Sundays.
SPENDING SPREE

Rents are creeping higher as the population expands rather than contracts. The stock market goes from strength to strength. Barely a day goes by without a new and ever glitzier restaurant opening its doors. A new nightclub district has mushroomed on the slopes above Hong Kong's business hub.
Shops are crammed, spending is up, life seems to be good.

"Hong Kong people are satisfied with their lives and with their government," said Michael DeGolyer, director of the 1997 Transition Project at Hong Kong's Baptist University, which has just issued the latest in a long series of public opinion polls.
"Clearly, Hong Kong people will regard this time as a Golden Sunset during which, in the opinion of the vast majority, life was good and so was the government," DeGolyer said.
But Hong Kong has had plenty of time to prepare for the red-letter moment -- and plenty of time to secure insurance, with some moving family members and assets offshore, just in case.
A DOZEN YEARS TO PREPARE
It's been more than 12 years since Britain and China signed the Joint Declaration in December 1984 sealing Hong Kong's fate.
Britain pledged to hand its last Asian outpost, a colony for nearly a century and a half, over to China when the clock strikes midnight on June 30, 1997.

China in turn vowed to allow this corner of untrammelled free trade considerable autonomy. Capitalism would prevail, Hong Kong people would run the place, neither communism nor officials from over the border would be grafted on to Hong Kong.

There are now only weeks to go until China's red flag rises over Hong Kong and these promises, codified in the Basic Law, a constitution promulgated by Beijing in 1990 to serve as a constitution, will be put to the test.

The symbols of the British empire are fast disappearing. The Queen's head has disappeared from coins and stamps. Victoria Park, named after the monarch who ruled when the British seized Hong Kong in 1841, will be renamed Central Park.

Hong Kong's first home-bred leader-in-waiting is assembling his team. Tung Chee-hwa, a Shanghai-born shipping magnate, was plucked from the business world by China in December to step into British Governor Chris Patten's shoes.
TWO OF PATTEN'S CHOICES RETAINED

Tung has selected his inner cabinet, or Executive Council, retaining two of Patten's choices and following the colonial practice of reserving three seats for Hong Kong's three most senior civil servants.
He has re-appointed the top tier of the powerful civil service to their posts, including the popular and influential Anson Chan, head of the civil service and deputy to Patten.
Whether they will all last for long remains to be seen. A question mark hangs over finance chief Donald Tsang, whose outspoken views have upset China, Hong Kong media say.

Tung's every action is being carefully scrutinised to see if he is his own man, capable of standing up against China, or if his hands are tied. Pro-democracy activists think he's China's man through and through.
But the public response in Hong Kong, newspaper polls show, has been one of general approval that Tung is embarking along a path of minimal change.
But DeGolyer warns that Hong Kong's confidence rests largely on the belief that Hong Kong will remain prosperous.
BASIS REMAINS

The basis is there. Earlier this month, Tsang revealed the British colony heads into the changeover cushioned by a record surplus of HK$15.1 billion (US$1.95 billion) for the current fiscal year ending on March 31.

When added to the rest of Hong Kong's reserves, the territory enters its new era with more that HK$330 billion in the bank. "The economic underpinning of confidence in Hong Kong's future cannot be overemphasised," DeGolyer said.
"Damage to Hong Kong's economic health, by economic mismanagement or political repression, would have extensive repercussions on the fundamental bases of confidence of the Hong Kong people."

The seeds of potential discord have been planted, liberal activists say. China's plans, endorsed by Tung, to roll back civil rights and dissolve the elected legislature have angered the pro-democracy lobby, which benefited from the electoral reforms by Patten, the 28th and last British governor.

The Democracy Party, Hong Kong's biggest, marked the one-year countdown with a candlelight vigil outside the Legislative Council building, greeting the stroke of midnight on 30 June 1996 with a chorus of "we shall overcome".
UNDOING REFORMS AT A STROKE
They will be kicked out of power in the legislature at the handover when an appointed provisional legislature is installed, undoing Patten's reforms at a stroke.
Democracy Party leader Martin Lee has embarked on exhaustive overseas lobbying to warn that the changes will snuff out Hong Kong's freedoms and inevitably damage prosperity.

This angered Tung, who accused Lee of "badmouthing" Hong Kong overseas. Tung now plans his own visit to the United States to explain, he says, that the changes are largely technical and will not materially affect Hong Kong's cherished freedoms.

If Hong Kong does unravel, it could come from a nervous but well-meaning China's meddling. The dead hand of central planning would mangle Hong Kong's economy, once compared to a delicate Swiss watch, political scientists say.
Or it could come from an angry Beijing crushing what it regards as a centre for subversion. Either way, if Hong Kong unravels, expect an exodus, they say.
Up to half a million Hong Kong people are estimated to have foreign passports -- many obtained after China bloodily crushed the Tiananmen Square democracy movement in 1989.
But up to half of the population of 6.4 million have kin or connections abroad that they believe can help extricate them if need be, said Hong Kong University political scientist Sunny Lo.
He said his research showed about 45 percent intended to decamp if Hong Kong goes sour. "I don't think the Tung Chee-hwa administration should underestimate this," he said.
